s: Which among the following is not a ‘constitutional provision for the formation of new States?
o: Increase the area of any State
Diminish the area of any State
Alter the name of any State
A State may include a Union territory
x: Under Article 3 of the Indian Constitution, only Parliament has been given the power to increase the area of any State, diminish the area of any State, alter the boundaries of any State and alter the name of any State (No state has the authority to include any territory by itself). Another thing is worth notice that Explanation 1 of Article 3 says that in this Article, in clauses (a) to (e) “State” includes a Union Territory but in the provison, “state” does not include a Union Territory. Thus, all the above options are true but (d) is a wrong statement. 17. Which of the following is NOT possible by a law of Parliament under Article 3 of the Constitution? (a) Formation of new States (b) Alteration of areas of States (c) Alteration of boundaries of States (d) Admission of new States U.P.P.C.S. (Pre) 2020 Ans. (d) Provisions for the formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing states come under Article 3. According to this Article, Parliament may by law: (a) form a new state by separation of territory from any state or by uniting two or more states or parts of states or by uniting any territory to a part of any state; (b) increase the area of any State; (c) diminish the area of any State; (d) alter the boundaries of any State; (e) alter the name of any State; Provision for admission or establishment of new States comes under Article 2 of the Indian Constitution. Thus, option (d) is the correct answer.

x: The Constitution of India contains all the usual features of a federation, viz, two governments, division of powers, written Constitution, rigidity of the Constitution, independent judiciary and Bi-cameralism. However, the Indian Constitution also contains a large no of unitary features, viz. a strong centre, single Constitution, single Citizenship, flexibility of Constitution, integrated Judiciary, appointment of state Governor by the centre, all India services, Emergency provision, etc.

s: Which one of the following determines that Indian Constitution is Federal?
o: Residuary powers are vested in centre/union
Distribution of powers between union and states
x: The democratic Governments are classified into two categories - Unitary and Federal. In a Unitary Constitution, all the powers are concentrated in a Central authority. The States are subordinated to such central authority. In a federal Constitution, there is a distribution of power among the Centre and the States. States are not subordinates of the Centre. In the Indian Constitution, there is a provision for the distribution of powers between the Union and States in the 7th Schedule, so it is called a Federal Constitution.

Wheare, in his book Federal Government, described the Indian System as “a quasi-federal state – a unitary state with subsidiary federal features.” Hence, he is cited as the originator of the concept of “Quasifederalism.” “Quasi-federal” implies a constitution containing both federal and unitary features, but with comparatively greater powers vested in the Centre.

s: What are Residuary subjects?
o: Subjects included in the State list
Subjects included in the Concurrent list
Subjects not included in any list
Subjects included in the Union list
x: Residuary subjects refer to matters that are not specifically mentioned in the Union List, State List, or Concurrent List under the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution. These subjects emerge due to changing circumstances, advancements in technology, or new policy needs. According to Article 248, the Parliament of India has exclusive power to legislate on these matters, meaning only the Union Legislature can make laws regarding them. Examples of residuary subjects include cyber laws, space research, atomic energy, artificial intelligence regulations, and foreign trade policies, as these areas were not foreseen when the Constitution was drafted. As new challenges arise, Parliament retains the authority to govern such subjects.
